hook.line: 144 mahjong tiles piled in a stack. Take them two by two, matching faces — can you clear it down to the last pair?
hook.say: Hi, Peacotile here! Let me show you the story of Shanghai.

ch.t: From mahjong tiles to a game for one
ch.say: The tiles were born in 19th-century China — the way to play, on a computer in 1981!
p: Mahjong is thought to have taken shape in the late 19th century, in the Qing era, on China's eastern coast. The oldest surviving tiles date from the 1870s, and Ningbo is known as its birthplace. In the 1920s it travelled from Shanghai to the West and became a worldwide craze.

The computer game that turned those tiles into a puzzle for one was made by the American Brodie Lockard: in 1981 he wrote “Mah-Jongg” on PLATO, an educational computer system. When Activision released it as “Shanghai” in 1986 it was a hit, and in Japan the game itself came to be called “Shanghai”.
st: Known as mahjong’s birthplace; tiles from this time survive

ch.t: Same faces, two at a time
ch.say: Only tiles with nothing on top and an open left or right side can go!
ch.cap: Only a tile with nothing on top and its left or right side open can be taken. The two glowing “Red Dragons” are a pair you can take now
p: From a stack of tiles several layers high you pick two with the same face and take them. A tile can go only if nothing lies on it and its left or right side is open. The flowers (plum, orchid, chrysanthemum, bamboo) and the seasons (spring, summer, autumn, winter) pair with their own kind, even with different pictures.

A set of 144 tiles: 36 each of characters, dots and bamboos, 16 winds, 12 dragons, and four flowers and four seasons. Take all 72 pairs to win — but in the wrong order you can run out of pairs at the end.
